claim: Lentiviral transgenesis using the HSP-tet construct generated lines with brain expression at a rate of 28.8%.
source: We found a construct containing the minimal HSP promoter most efficiently generated lines with specific expression patterns in brain (28.8%, see Table 1)
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific percentage (28.8%) and references Table 1 which contains the data showing 38 lines with expression out of 132 analyzed for HSP-tet construct.

claim: The PiggyBac transposon system has a weaker tendency to undergo local hops compared to the SleepingBeauty transposon.
source: Unlike the SleepingBeauty transposon, PiggyBac has a weaker tendency to undergo local hops (Liang et al., 2009, but see supplemental note)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Liang et al., 2009, though the authors note there is additional discussion in the supplemental note.

claim: More than 200 independent PiggyBac lines were established.
source: We established more than 200 independent lines and examined expression patterns from more than 130 lines (210 and 135 as of October 2015, respectively; see Supplementary file 1 for line expression summary and insertion sites).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of lines established (210 as of October 2015).

claim: The rate of obtaining lines with brain expression in the PB screen (78.5%) was more than twice that obtained with lentiviral transgenesis.
source: The rate of obtaining lines with brain expression in the PB screen (78.5% ) was more than twice that obtained with lentiviral transgenesis (Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages and references Table 1 which shows 124 lines with expression out of 158 analyzed for PiggyBac constructs (78.5%).

claim: Line 48L has expression in limbic cortex layer 5 pyramidal cells.
source: 48L has expression in limbic cortex (A1, coronal section) layer 5 pyramidal cells (A2, magnified image in limbic cortex).
evidence: The claim is supported by both text description and Figure 1A showing the expression pattern.

claim: Line TCBV shows columnar axons from retina in the superior colliculus.
source: Superior colliculus (SC) of TCBV has columnar axons from retina. B1: sagittal section, B2: magnified image of superior colliculus.
evidence: The claim is supported by text description and Figure 1B showing the axonal projections.

claim: Line 52L has expression in Cajal-Retzius cells in the dentate gyrus and cerebral cortex.
source: 52L has expression in piriform cortex (see Figure 9) and Cajal-Retzius cells in dentate gyrus (DG, C2) and cerebral cortex (C3, inset: magnified image of a Cajal-Retzius cell).
evidence: The claim is supported by text description and Figure 1C showing expression in Cajal-Retzius cells.

claim: Line TCGS has expression in layer 4 neurons of primary sensory cortices including primary somatosensory, visual, and auditory areas.
source: TCGS has expression in layer 4 neurons of primary sensory cortices (primary somatosensory area: SSp and primary visual area:VISp in D3).
evidence: The claim is supported by text description and Figure 1D showing layer 4 expression in primary sensory cortices.

claim: Line TCFQ has nearly complementary layer 4 expression excluding primary sensory cortices.
source: TCFQ which was devoid of expression in primary sensory cortices but expressed in associative cortices (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by text description and Figure 1E showing expression pattern complementary to TCGS.

claim: Line TCJD has expression in the dorsal part of the lateral geniculate nucleus which projects to primary visual cortex.
source: TCJD has expression in dorsal part of lateral geniculate nucleus (LGd, F1), which projects to primary visual cortex (VISp). F1: sagittal section, F2: higher magnification of LGd, F3: higher magnification of axons in layers 1, 4, and 6 of VISp.
evidence: The claim is supported by text description and Figure 1F showing expression in LGd and projections to VISp.

claim: Tet reporter expression could be turned off and on by administration of doxycycline.
source: Tet reporter expression could be turned off and on by administration of doxycycline (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by text and Figure 1—figure supplement 3 showing doxycycline-dependent control of reporter expression.

claim: Lentiviral transgenesis requires viral injection into single cell embryos and transfer to a foster mother for each new founder.
source: Generation of each new founder requires viral injection into single cell embryos and transfer of that embryo to a foster mother (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the procedural requirements for lentiviral transgenesis.

claim: Four lentiviral lines lost expression in the founder and early progeny in later generations, implying possible silencing of lentiviral transgenes over generations.
source: Moreover, we found four lines in which expression in the founder and early progeny was lost in later generations, implying possible silencing of lentiviral transgenes over generations (Hofmann et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript reports observational data of expression loss and cites Hofmann et al., 2006 for the silencing phenomenon.

claim: Viruses with insulator sequences had 100 times lower titer (about 1 x 10^7 infection unit/ml) and were not usable for transgenesis.
source: We tried to incorporate insulator sequences (see below) to prevent silencing, but viruses with insulator sequences had 100 times lower titer (about 1 x 107 infection unit/ml) and were not usable for transgenesis.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific titer measurements and practical outcome.

claim: Five PiggyBac seed lines with single-copy insertions were established from 28 PB-positive animals.
source: Among 28 PB-positive animals, five had single-copy insertions confirmed by quantitative PCR and ligation-mediated PCR. These five served as seed lines for subsequent rounds of piggyBac transgenesis.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numbers of animals and seed lines established.

claim: Prm-PBase produced founders more efficiently than Rosa-PBase.
source: We found that Prm-PBase produced founders more efficiently than Rosa-PBase (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Table 2 showing higher efficiency of new line production with Prm-PBase.

claim: The PB allele transmission rate was significantly lower than the expected Mendelian ratio, implying that a substantial fraction of excised PB failed to re-insert into the host genome.
source: We found that the PB allele transmission rate was significantly lower than the expected Mendelian ratio, implying that a substantial fraction of excised PB failed to re-insert into the host genome (Table 2).
evidence: The manuscript provides interpretation of transmission rate data from Table 2.

claim: The proportion of insertions into genes (35.9%) was comparable to that expected by chance (33.3%).
source: The proportion of insertions into genes (60/167, 35.9% ) was comparable to that expected by chance (33.3% (Liang et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages and compares to published expected values.

claim: On average, more than three times fewer structures were labeled in PB lines (33) than in Cre lines (107).
source: We found that, on average, more than three times fewer structures were labeled in PB lines (33) than in the Cre lines (107) (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numbers and references Figure 3 showing the distribution.

claim: PB lines had expression bias to forebrain structures such as the isocortex, olfactory bulb, and hippocampus.
source: Cre lines had relatively homogenous expression rates (70–83% ) in any brain regions, whereas PB lines had expression bias to forebrain structures such as the isocortex, olfactory bulb, and hippocampus (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D comparing expression rates across brain regions.

claim: Some PB lines (24/135) had expression in tissues other than the brain, including skin, bone, viscera, and adipocytes.
source: Although our screen was focused on brain expression, we also performed a brief screen of the rest of the body and found that some lines (24/135) also had expression in tissues other than the brain, including skin (8), bone (5), viscera (9), and brown (1) and white (3) adipocytes.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific counts of lines with non-brain expression.

claim: A few PB lines showed variable expression patterns in individual animals.
source: A few lines showed variable expression patterns in individual animals. P039 had stable expression in subiculum, but its expression in cortex varied, and two lines (P027 and P197) had expression that was left-right asymmetric.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific examples of lines with variable expression.

claim: Many PB lines showed different reporter expression patterns at different ages, likely reflecting the developmental dynamics of the trapped enhancers.
source: Many lines showed different reporter expression patterns at different ages, likely reflecting the developmental dynamics of the trapped enhancers.
evidence: The manuscript provides interpretation of age-dependent expression changes.

claim: Among 34 lines examined for adult expression, mature expression was reduced in 12 lines but retained in 22 lines.
source: Screening was primarily carried out in young adults (P20-30). We examined adult (P50 or later) expression in 34 lines. Mature expression was reduced in 12 of these lines, but was retained in the remaining 22 lines.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific counts of lines with different developmental expression patterns.

claim: Line P162 showed complex spatiotemporal expression patterns with different structures expressing at different developmental stages.
source: Some lines showed complex spatiotemporal expression patterns. For example, young postnatal animals (P10-12) from line P162 had expression in primary sensory cortices, the parafascicular nucleus of the thalamus and pontine grey, but more mature (3 weeks or older) animals lost thalamic and pontine expression and gained subiculum expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), suggesting the probe trapped enhancer(s) activated in different structures at different developmental stages.
evidence: The claim is supported by text description and Figure 2—figure supplement 2 showing age-dependent expression changes.

claim: Silencing of PB transgenes over generations was not observed, unlike some lentiviral lines.
source: Unlike some lentiviral lines, silencing of PB transgenes over generations was not observed; even lines losing expression late in adulthood had pups that regained reporter expression.
evidence: The manuscript reports observational data comparing PB and lentiviral line stability.

claim: AAV-TRE-driven mCherry reporter was expressed specifically in mCitrine-positive cells in most cases.
source: We injected adenoassociated virus (AAV) encoding TRE-driven transgenes into multiple areas in different lines (Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and Figure 10. See Figure 2—source data 1 for counts). We found mCherry reporter was expressed specifically expressed in mCitrine-positive cells in most of cases.
evidence: The claim is supported by text and figures showing viral reporter expression patterns.

claim: Infection efficiency of AAV-TRE constructs varied from 36.5% to nearly 100% depending on the line and brain region.
source: Infection efficiency varied from 36.5% (CA1 pyramidal cells in P066, Figure 2—figure supplement 4D) to nearly 100% (layer 6 pyramidal cells in 56L, Figure 10R and T), probably due to AAV serotype preference.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages and references figures showing infection efficiency.

claim: A small percentage (0.7% ± 0.7%) of AAV-infected cells were mCitrine-negative but in the same layer/positions as mCitrine-positive cells.
source: In some lines, as reported (Choy, 2015), we found a few viral reporter-positive but mCitrine-negative cells in the same layer/positions with those of mCitrine-positive cells (arrowheads in Figure 2—figure supplement 3E and F; 0.7% +/- 0.7% of infected cells, n=6 injections in 5 strains), but never in ectopic positions lacking mCitrine positive cells.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentage and sample size for off-target expression.

claim: TREtight-myrmCherry-HA was expressed only in mCitrine-positive cells and could be used to map axonal projections.
source: Myristoylated mCherry driven by a second-generation TRE (TREtight-myrmCherry-HA) was expressed only in mCitrine-positive cells and could be used to map their axonal projections (see below).
evidence: The manuscript describes the specificity and utility of this construct.

claim: TREtight-ChR2H134R-mCherry had specific expression only in mCitrine-positive cells and could drive action potentials upon blue light stimulation.
source: Similarly, tet-dependent channelrhodopsin virus (TREtight-ChR2H134R-mCherry) had specific expression only in mCitrine-positive cells and could drive action potentials upon blue light stimulation (Choy, 2015).
evidence: The manuscript describes the specificity and functionality of this construct, citing Choy, 2015.

claim: Nearly all attempts to use TRE to drive recombinase expression were unsuccessful due to low level leak combined with high sensitivity of cre-dependent recombination.
source: Nearly all these attempts were unsuccessful (see Figure 2—figure supplement 4 and 5) due first to low level leak of all versions of the TRE promoter tried, combined with the high sensitivity of cre-dependent recombination.
evidence: The manuscript describes the technical challenges encountered with multiple constructs.

claim: GFP nanobody-split Cre virus achieved specific Cre-reporter expression restricted to mCitrine-positive cells.
source: We were able to obtain specific Cre-reporter expression restricted to mCitrine-positive cells, using an implementation of the GFP nanobody-split Cre virus (developed independently from Tang et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript describes successful implementation of this approach, citing Tang et al., 2015.

claim: Line P172 has layer 4 expression in three primary sensory cortices (primary somatosensory, visual, and auditory areas).
source: P172 (Figure 4A) had layer 4 expression in three primary sensory cortices (primary somatosensory area: SSp, primary visual area: VISp, and primary auditory area: AUDp)
evidence: The claim is supported by text description and Figure 4A showing the expression pattern.

claim: Line P063 has layer 4 expression only in primary auditory cortex.
source: P063 (Figure 4B), and P160 (Figure 4C) has expression in only in AUDp and VISp layer 4 neurons respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by text description and Figure 4B showing the expression pattern.

claim: Line P160 has layer 4 expression only in primary visual cortex.
source: P063 (Figure 4B), and P160 (Figure 4C) has expression in only in AUDp and VISp layer 4 neurons respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by text description and Figure 4C showing the expression pattern.

claim: Layer 5 pyramidal neurons are categorized by their axonal projection patterns and somatodendritic morphologies.
source: Layer 5 pyramidal neurons are categorized by their axonal projection patterns and somatodendritic morphologies (Hattox and Nelson, 2007; Molyneaux et al., 2007): callosal neurons (projecting to contralateral cortex) have thinner apical dendrites and smaller somata, whereas corticofugal (subcereberal) projection neurons have thick tufted dendrites and larger somata.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hattox and Nelson, 2007 and Molyneaux et al., 2007.

claim: Line P136 has expression in callosal thin tufted pyramidal neurons located in upper layer 5 (layer 5a) and projecting to the entire caudoputamen.
source: P136 (Figure 4D) has expression in callosal thin tufted pyramidal neurons located in upper layer 5 (layer 5a) and projecting to the entire caudoputamen.
evidence: The claim is supported by text description and Figure 4D showing the expression and projection pattern.

claim: Line P161 has expression in callosal projecting thin-tufted cells forming a thin layer above layer 6.
source: P161 (Figure 4E) has expression in callosal projecting thin-tufted cells forming a thin layer above layer 6.
evidence: The claim is supported by text description and Figure 4E showing the expression pattern.

claim: Line P074 has expression in callosal projecting pyramidal neurons in anterior (motor and somatosensory) cortex with axonal projections biased to lateral caudoputamen.
source: P074 (Figure 4F) has expression in callosal projecting pyramidal neurons in anterior (motor and somatosensory) cortex with axonal projections that are biased to lateral caudoputamen.
evidence: The claim is supported by text description and Figure 4F showing the expression and projection pattern.

claim: Thick tufted cortico-tectal neuronal lines (P081 and P084) showed differences in regional expression patterns.
source: Thick tufted cortico-tectal neuronal lines (P081 and P084, Figure 4G and H) and cortico-spinal lines (P149 and P135, Figure 4I and J) also showed differences in regional expression patterns (P081: strong in somatomotor (MO) and supplemental somatomoter area (SSs), P084: only in SSp, P149: strong in MO and SSs, P135: SSp and VISp).
evidence: The claim is supported by text description and Figures 4G-J showing different regional patterns.

claim: Line P152 has expression in the glomerular layer of the main olfactory bulb with dendrites pointing toward the centers of glomeruli, characteristic of periglomerular cells.
source: P152 and P110 have expression in the glomerular layer of the main olfactory bulb (MOBgl). mCitrine-positive cells' dendrites point toward the centers of glomeruli in P152 (Figure 5A), but dendrites are mainly confined to glomerulus walls in P110 (Figure 5B). These morphological differences are characteristic of periglomerular cells and superficial short axon cells, respectively (Nagayama et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by text description, Figure 5A, and citation to Nagayama et al., 2014 for cell type identification.

claim: Line P110 has expression in the glomerular layer of the main olfactory bulb with dendrites mainly confined to glomerulus walls, characteristic of superficial short axon cells.
source: P152 and P110 have expression in the glomerular layer of the main olfactory bulb (MOBgl). mCitrine-positive cells' dendrites point toward the centers of glomeruli in P152 (Figure 5A), but dendrites are mainly confined to glomerulus walls in P110 (Figure 5B). These morphological differences are characteristic of periglomerular cells and superficial short axon cells, respectively (Nagayama et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by text description, Figure 5B, and citation to Nagayama et al., 2014 for cell type identification.

claim: Line P157 has mCitrine-positive cells confined to the basal half of the outer plexiform layer of the main olfactory bulb.
source: There are several lines with expression in the outer plexiform layer (MOBopl). Many of these lines have an even distribution of labeled cell bodies within the MOBopl (P118 Figure 5C) but P157 (Figure 5D) has mCitrine-positive cells confined to the basal half of the layer.
evidence: The claim is supported by text description and Figure 5D showing the restricted expression pattern.

claim: The entorhinal cortex, hippocampus, and subiculum are interconnected by complex loops with reciprocal connections.
source: The entorhinal cortex, hippocampus, and subiculum are interconnected by complex loops with reciprocal connections (Ding, 2013; Witter et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ding, 2013 and Witter et al., 2014.

claim: Many (92) PB lines have expression in subregions of the hippocampal formation.
source: Many (92) lines have expression in subregions of the hippocampal formation.
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific count of lines with hippocampal formation expression.

claim: Lines P162, P139, and P141 label cells proximal to CA1 that do not project to the presubiculum.
source: Labeled cells proximal to CA1 in three lines, P162 (Figure 6A), P139 (Figure 6B), and P141 (Figure 6C), do not project to PRE but the distal subiculum population labeled in P157 (Figure 6D) does.
evidence: The claim is supported by text description and Figures 6A-C showing lack of PRE projections.

claim: Line P157 labels distal subiculum population that projects to the presubiculum.
source: Labeled cells proximal to CA1 in three lines, P162 (Figure 6A), P139 (Figure 6B), and P141 (Figure 6C), do not project to PRE but the distal subiculum population labeled in P157 (Figure 6D) does.
evidence: The claim is supported by text description and Figure 6D showing PRE projections.

claim: Line P162 has dense mCitrine-positive axons in the reuniens nucleus and dorsal and ventral submedial nucleus, unlike P139 and P141.
source: P162, P139, and P141 have expression in adjacent positions (cells in P162 and P139 are in nearly the same positions and P141 cells are located posterior to them, (see distal ends of CA1 marked by arrowheads in Figure 6A–C) but have different axonal projections. P162 has dense mCitrine-positive axons in the reuniens nucleus (RE) and dorsal and ventral submedial nucleus (SMT) but there are few axons in the corresponding areas in P139 and P141 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by text description and Figure 6—figure supplement 1 showing differential projection patterns.

claim: Injection of tet-dependent virus into the subiculum in P162 confirmed that axons in RE and SMT were coming from the subiculum.
source: Injection of tet –dependent virus (AAV-Tre3G-myristylated mCherry-HA) into the subiculum in P162 confirmed that axons in RE and SMT were coming from the subiculum (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by text description and Figure 6—figure supplement 1G-I showing viral tracing results.

claim: Line P138 labels the endopiriform nucleus separately from the claustrum.
source: We identified lines separately labeling endopiriform nucleus (P138, Figure 7A) and claustrum (P018, Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by text description and Figure 7A showing specific endopiriform expression.

claim: Line P018 labels the claustrum.
source: We identified lines separately labeling endopiriform nucleus (P138, Figure 7A) and claustrum (P018, Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by text description and Figure 7B showing claustrum expression.

claim: Line P170 has expression in the anterior part of the basolateral amygdalar nucleus.
source: P170 has expression in the anterior part of the basolateral amygdalar nucelus (BLA, Figure 7C)
evidence: The claim is supported by text description and Figure 7C showing BLA expression.

claim: Line P113 shows complementary expression in lateral and basomedial amygdalar nuclei.
source: P113 shows complementally expression in lateral and basomedial amygdalar nuclei (BLA and BMA, Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by text description and Figure 7D showing LA and BMA expression.

claim: There are 29 PB lines with expression in striatum and related structures.
source: There are 29 lines with expression in striatum and related structures.
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific count of lines with striatal expression.

claim: Line P172 has expression in the striosomes in dorsal caudoputamen projecting to both globus pallidus external part and substantia nigra reticular part.
source: P172 has expression in the striasomes in dorsal caudoputamen projecting to both globus pallidus, external part (GPe) and substantia nigra, reticular part (SNr) (Figure 7G).
evidence: The claim is supported by text description and Figure 7G showing striosome expression and projections.

claim: Striatal mCitrine-expressing cells in P118 are biased toward the anterior caudoputamen and appear to consist mainly of indirect pathway cells projecting to GPe.
source: Striatal mCitrine-expressing cells in P118 are biased toward the anterior caudoputamen and appear to consist mainly of indirect pathway cells projecting to GPe (Figure 7H).
evidence: The claim is supported by text description and Figure 7H showing anterior striatal expression and GPe projections.

claim: Line P170 had sexually dimorphic expression with males but not females having expression in the medial preoptic area.
source: P170 had sexually dimorphic expression; males (Figure 7M1) but not females (Figure 7M2) had expression in the medial preoptic area (MPO) and bed nuclei of stria terminalis (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by text description and Figures 7M1-M2 showing sex-dependent expression.

claim: Both MPO and bed nuclei of stria terminalis are larger in males than females.
source: Since both structures are larger in males than females (Cooke et al., 1998) further work will be needed to determine if the neurons themselves or only their reporter expression are sexually dimorphic.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Cooke et al., 1998.

claim: Line P066 has expression in neurons of the inferior olivary complex which send climbing fibers to the cerebellum.
source: P066 has expression in neurons of the inferior olivary complex (IO), which send climbing fibers to the cerebellum (Figure 7R).
evidence: The claim is supported by text description and Figure 7R showing IO expression and cerebellar projections.

claim: Line P014 has restricted expression in Purkinje cells occupying a stripe-like pattern that is consistent across individuals.
source: Expression in Purkinje cells in P014 was restricted to a small subset occupying a stripe-like pattern (Figure 8C) that is consistent across individuals (Figure 8C inset).
evidence: The claim is supported by text description and Figure 8C showing the stripe pattern and consistency.

claim: Line P033 has restricted expression in granule cells that project to the basal half of the molecular layer.
source: P033 has restricted expression in granule cells that project to the basal half of the molecular layer.
evidence: The manuscript describes the specific projection pattern of P033 granule cells.

claim: Lines P134 and P159 have cell bodies directly beneath the Purkinje cell layer and extend dendrites into the molecular layer, appearing to be Lugaro cells.
source: There were two lines (P134 and P159) that have cell bodies directly beneath the Purkinje cell layer and extend dendrites into the molecular layer (Figure 8J–L). From their cell body positions and morphology, they appear to be Lugaro cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by text description and Figures 8J-L showing morphology consistent with Lugaro cells.

claim: Three lines (48L, 52L, P113) have distinctive expression patterns in the cell-dense layer (layer II) of the piriform cortex.
source: We found three lines (48L, 52L, P113) with distinctive expression patterns in the cell-dense layer (layer II) of the piriform cortex (Figure 9A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by text description and Figures 9A-C showing different piriform cortex layer II patterns.

claim: Two broad categories of layer II glutamatergic neurons have previously been described in piriform cortex: semilunar cells and superficial pyramidal cells.
source: Two broad categories of layer II glutamatergic neurons have previously been described; semilunar (SL) cells, which lack well-defined basal dendrites and are located in the upper sublayer of layer II, and superficial pyramidal (SP) cells, which, like most pyramids, possess distinct basal and apical dendrites and are located deeper in layer II (Suzuki and Bekkers, 2006; 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Suzuki and Bekkers, 2006 and 2011.

claim: 48L cells were recently shown to be a subset of semilunar cells.
source: 48L cells were recently shown to be a subset of SL cells (Choy, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Choy, 2015.

claim: Based on cell body positions and dendritic morphology, the labeled cells in P113 appear to be typical superficial pyramidal cells.
source: Based on their cell body positions (Figure 9D) and dendritic morphology, the labeled cells in P113 appear to be typical SP cells.
evidence: The claim is based on morphological analysis shown in Figure 9D.

claim: 52L cells were GABA-negative but do not clearly match the anatomical and physiological properties of either subtype of previously described pyramidal neurons.
source: 52L cells were GABA-negative (data not shown) but do not clearly match the anatomical and physiological properties of either subtype of previously described pyramidal neurons.
evidence: The manuscript reports GABA staining results and comparison to known cell types.

claim: 52L labeled cells and non-labeled cells in piriform cortex differ significantly in mean firing frequencies, AHP amplitude, and instantaneous firing frequencies.
source: Average F–I curves (I), AHP amplitude (J), and instantaneous firing frequency (K) for labeled cells (red) and non-labeled cells (black) were significantly different (asterisks): mean firing frequencies (averaged over 400–500 pA current injection, 11 ± 5 Hz and 28 ± 5 Hz, p = 0.025), AHP amplitude (-1.2 ± 0.3 mV and -3.4 ± 0.6 mV, p=0.0073, labeled and non-labeled cells, respectively), and in instantaneous firing frequencies (131 ± 12 Hz and 58 ± 10 Hz, p = 0.00019). n= 10 for each; line.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of physiological recordings shown in Figures 9I-K.

claim: 52L labeled neurons possess basal dendrites but do not have a distinct apical dendrite, unlike typical superficial pyramidal cells.
source: Morphologically, the non-labeled neurons resemble previously described SP cells since they possessed distinct basal and apical dendrites (Figure 9H). Labeled neurons also possessed basal dendrites (unlike SL cells) but do not have a distinct apical dendrite (Figure 9F).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figures 9F and 9H.

claim: 52L cells are a distinct subset of superficial pyramidal cells that differ phenotypically from other, unlabeled superficial pyramidal cells.
source: Taken together, our anatomical and physiological results suggest that 52L cells are a distinct subset of SP cells that differ phenotypically from other, unlabeled SP cells.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the anatomical and physiological data presented.

claim: Single cell tracing has shown that there are two types of layer 6 cortico-thalamic projecting pyramidal neurons.
source: Single cell tracing has shown that there are two types of L6 CT projecting pyramidal neurons (Thomson, 2010; Zhang and Deschenes, 1997)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Thomson, 2010 and Zhang and Deschenes, 1997.

claim: Primary sensory cortico-thalamic pyramidal neurons send axons to primary sensory thalamic nuclei.
source: primary sensory CT pyramidal neurons send axons to primary sensory thalamic nuclei (ex. ventro-posterior medial:VPm, lateral geniculate dorsal nucleus: LGd).
evidence: The claim describes established knowledge about primary CT neuron projections.

claim: Non-primary cortico-thalamic neurons send weaker projections to primary sensory nuclei but also project to secondary sensory nuclei.
source: Non-primary CT neurons send weaker projections to primary sensory nuclei, but also project to secondary sensory nuclei; for example, in primary somatosensory cortex, they send axons to VPM, posterior thalamic nuclei (Po), and intralaminar thalamic nucleus.
evidence: The claim describes established knowledge about non-primary CT neuron projections.

claim: Primary cortico-thalamic neurons are located in upper layer 6 and non-primary cortico-thalamic neurons in lower layer 6.
source: Primary CT neurons are located in upper layer 6 and non-primary CT neurons in lower layer 6.
evidence: The claim describes established knowledge about CT neuron laminar positions.

claim: Primary cortico-thalamic neurons project to the thalamic reticular nucleus, whereas non-primary cortico-thalamic neurons do not.
source: Primary CT neurons also project to the thalamic reticular nucleus (RTN), whereas non-primary CT neurons do not.
evidence: The claim describes established knowledge about differential RTN projections.

claim: Primary cortico-thalamic neurons extend apical dendrites to layer 4 while dendrites of non-primary cortico-thalamic neurons do not reach layer 4.
source: Primary CT neurons extend apical dendrites to layer 4 while dendrites of non-primary CT neurons do not reach to layer 4.
evidence: The claim describes established knowledge about CT neuron dendritic morphology.

claim: Three PB lines (P162, P139, 56L) were obtained with expression in layer 6 cortical pyramidal neurons.
source: We obtained three lines with expression in layer 6 cortical pyramidal neurons (Figure 10).
evidence: The claim is supported by text and Figure 10 showing the three lines.

claim: Line P162 has mCitrine-positive cells in primary somatosensory area, primary visual area, and retrosplenial cortex with axonal projection in VPm and LGd.
source: P162 has mCitrine-positive cells in primary somatosensory area (SSp), primary visual area (VISp), and retrosplenical cortex and axonal projection in VPm and LGd (Figure 10G–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by text description and Figures 10G-J showing expression and projections.

claim: Line P139 has expression in lateral cortex including supplemental somatosensory area and gustatory cortex with projection in Po.
source: P139 has expression in lateral cortex including supplemental somatosensory area (SSs) and gustatory cortex and projection in Po (Figure 10M–P).
evidence: The claim is supported by text description and Figures 10M-P showing expression and projections.

claim: There are topological projection patterns in RTN with dorsally located P162 cells projecting to dorsal RTN and laterally located P139 cells projecting to ventral RTN.
source: There are topological projection patterns in RTN; dorsally located P162 cells project to dorsal RTN and laterally located P139 cells project to ventral RTN (Figure 10—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by text description and Figure 10—figure supplement 1B-C showing topological projections.

claim: Line 56L has broad expression across neocortex with projection to both primary and secondary nuclei but not to RTN.
source: The third line, 56L, has broad expression across neocortex (Figure 10A–D). 56L neurons have projection to both primary and secondary nuclei but not to RTN (Figure 10—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by text description and Figures 10A-D and Figure 10—figure supplement 1A showing expression and projections.

claim: Cell bodies of P162 and P139 are located in upper layer 6, but those of 56L are in lower layer 6.
source: Cell bodies of P162 and P139 are located in upper layer 6, but those of 56L are in lower layer 6 (Figure 10—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by text description and Figure 10—figure supplement 2A-B showing cell body positions.

claim: P162 and P139 have apical dendrites reaching to layer 4, with some extending to layer 1.
source: P162 and P139 have apical dendrites reaching to layer 4 (Figure 10K, L and Q); some apical dendrites even extended to layer 1 (Figure 10K).
evidence: The claim is supported by text description and Figures 10K, L, and Q showing dendritic morphology.

claim: 56L dendrites in SSp did not step into layer 4, but in VISp some neurons extended dendrites to layer 1.
source: On the other hand, 56L dendrites in SSp did not step in to layer 4. In VISp, some neurons extended dendrites to layer 1.
evidence: The manuscript describes the dendritic patterns of 56L in different cortical areas.

claim: From their cell body locations and projection patterns, P162 and P139 appeared to be primary-CT type pyramidal neurons in different cortical areas.
source: From their cell body locations and projection patterns, P162 and P139 appeared to be primary-CT type pyramidal neurons in different cortical areas.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the anatomical data presented.

claim: 56L cells have larger whole cell capacitances than P162 and P139 cells and tended to have correspondingly lower input resistances.
source: 56L cells have larger whole cell capacitances than P162 and P139 cells and tended to have correspondingly lower input resistances.
evidence: The manuscript reports physiological measurements comparing the three lines.

claim: All mCitrine-positive cells in P162, P139, and 56L fired tonically.
source: All mCitrine-positive cells fired tonically (Figure 10—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by text and Figure 10—figure supplement 2C-D showing firing patterns.

claim: Most mCitrine-negative cells recorded near mCitrine-positive cells in 56L fired more phasically and at lower rates.
source: In the 56L recordings, we found that most mCitrine-negative cells recorded near mCitrine-positive cells fired more phasically and at lower rates (Figure 10—figure supplement 2F–H) reminiscent of the firing previously described for CC cells (Mercer et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by text, Figure 10—figure supplement 2F-H, and citation to Mercer et al., 2005.

claim: Labeled axons from 56L SSp cells were found in Po, VPM, and the intralaminar nucleus, consistent with previously described projections of non-primary CT cells.
source: In contrast, labeled axons from 56L SSp cells (Figure 10R and S) were found in Po, VPM, and the intralaminar nucleus (ILM), consistent with previously described projections of non-primary CT cells (Zhang and Deschenes, 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by text, Figures 10R-S, and citation to Zhang and Deschenes, 1997.

claim: 56L had long lateral axonal projections that reached to the contralateral hemisphere, whereas P162 and P139 cells had local lateral axonal projections within the cerebral cortex.
source: We also found that 56L had long lateral axonal projections that even reached to the contralateral hemisphere, whereas P162 and P139 cells had local lateral axonal projections within the cerebral cortex (Figure 10—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by text and Figure 10—figure supplement 4 showing differential projection patterns.

claim: Clustering samples by correlations between gene expression vectors revealed two main clusters: those from 56L and all others.
source: Clustering samples by correlations between gene expression vectors revealed two main clusters: those from 56L and all others (Figure 11A).
evidence: The claim is supported by text and Figure 11A showing the clustering analysis.

claim: Samples from P162 and P139 are intermingled in the cluster, implying they have quite similar RNA expression profiles.
source: Samples from P162 and P139 are intermingled in the cluster, implying they have quite similar RNA expression profiles.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the clustering analysis shown in Figure 11A.

claim: There were 1869 genes differentially expressed among all sample groups (false discovery rate < 0.01).
source: There were 1869 genes differentially expressed among all sample groups (false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.01), and most differentially expressed genes showed bimodal patterns; high expressions in one group and low expressions in the other (Figure 11B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by text and Figures 11B-C showing differential gene expression analysis.

claim: Most differentially expressed genes showed bimodal patterns with high expressions in one group and low expressions in the other.
source: There were 1869 genes differentially expressed among all sample groups (false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.01), and most differentially expressed genes showed bimodal patterns; high expressions in one group and low expressions in the other (Figure 11B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by text and Figures 11B-C showing the expression patterns.

claim: Tle4 and Bmp3 have essentially non-overlapping expression in layer 6.
source: We confirmed the expression of Tle4 (which is expressed strongly in Ntsr1-cre) and Bmp3 (expressed in 56L) by dual-color in situ hybridization. Tle4 and Bmp3 have essentially non-overlapping expression (Figure 11D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by text and Figures 11D-F showing dual-color in situ hybridization results.

claim: mCitrine-positive cells in P162 and P139 dominantly express Tle4 with only a few Bmp3-positive cells.
source: mCitrine-positive cells in P162 and P139 dominantly express Tle4 with only a few Bmp3-positive cells, whereas 56L cells are mostly Bmp3-positive but Tle4-negative (Figure 11G–O).
evidence: The claim is supported by text and Figures 11G-O showing in situ hybridization results.

claim: 56L cells are mostly Bmp3-positive but Tle4-negative.
source: mCitrine-positive cells in P162 and P139 dominantly express Tle4 with only a few Bmp3-positive cells, whereas 56L cells are mostly Bmp3-positive but Tle4-negative (Figure 11G–O).
evidence: The claim is supported by text and Figures 11G-O showing in situ hybridization results.

claim: In all three lines (P162, P139, 56L), the majority of marker (Tle4 or Bmp3)-positive cells do not express mCitrine, suggesting the three lines label subsets of these marker-positive cells.
source: In all lines, the majority of marker (Tle4 or Bmp3)-positive cells do not express mCitrine, suggesting the three lines label subsets of these marker-positive cells.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the in situ hybridization data.

claim: 100% (333/333) of Tdtomato+ cells in Ntsr1-Cre;Ai14 animals were Tle4+ and 77.8% (333/428) of Tle4+ cells were TdTomato+.
source: We also analyzed Tle4 expression in the Ntsr1-Cre animal (Nstr1-Cre;Ai14 Rosa-TdTomato) from dual-fluorescent in situ images (http://connectivity.brain-map.org/transgenic/experiment/100147520) and found Ntsr1-Cre cells co-expressed Tle4; 100% (333/333) of Tdtomato+ cells were Tle4+ and 77.8% (333/428) of Tle4+ cells were TdTomato+.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of publicly available in situ data.

claim: P162 and P139 are subsets of the Ntsr1-cre population and 56L cells are a distinct population of layer 6 cortico-thalamic neurons.
source: These results support the view that P162 and P139 are subsets of the Ntsr1-cre population and that 56L cells are a distinct population of L6 CT neurons.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the combined anatomical, physiological, and molecular data.

claim: The enhancer trap approach produces more focused labeling than commonly used approaches that attempt to recapitulate known patterns of endogenous gene expression.
source: The enhancer trap approach produces more focused labeling than commonly used approaches that attempt to recapitulate known patterns of endogenous gene expression.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the comparative analysis with BAC-Cre lines shown in Figure 3.

claim: Cell-type-specific patterns of gene expression are thought to reflect interactions between regulatory sequences within the proximal promoter and at other far more distal sites.
source: Cell-type-specific patterns of gene expression are thought to reflect interactions between regulatory sequences within the proximal promoter, and at other far more distal sites (Nathanson et al., 2009; Pennacchio et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nathanson et al., 2009 and Pennacchio et al., 2006.

claim: Single genes often have multiple enhancer modules each of which regulates expression in different regional or developmental contexts.
source: Single genes often have multiple enhancer modules each of which regulates expression in different regional or developmental contexts (Dickel et al., 2013; Visel et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dickel et al., 2013 and Visel et al., 2009.

claim: Hopping from single copy PB enabled fast identification of insertion sites without the laborious and time-consuming steps of tracking and segregating multiple transgene alleles.
source: Hopping from single copy PB enabled fast identification of insertion sites without the laborious and time-consuming steps of tracking and segregating multiple transgene alleles.
evidence: This is a summary of the methodological advantage of the PiggyBac approach.

claim: The strategy of including a mCitrine reporter on the probe enables fast expression screening without crossing to a separate reporter line.
source: Our strategy of including a mCitrine reporter on the probe enables fast expression screening without crossing to a separate reporter line, and including tTA enables inducible genetic manipulation in specifically labeled populations.
evidence: This describes a design feature of the enhancer trap system.

claim: Most PB lines maintain consistent expression over generations.
source: Although our enhancer trap lines were generated by random insertion, most lines maintain consistent expression over generations.
evidence: This is a summary of the stability data presented earlier.

claim: Lines generated by local hopping have similar expression patterns, supporting that expression patterns are tightly linked to transgenes' insertion sites.
source: In addition, lines generated by local hopping have similar expression patterns. These facts support the conclusion that the expression patterns are not generated randomly, but instead are tightly linked to transgenes' insertion sites.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the local hopping data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: PB translocation sites were widely distributed over the genome and lines with insertions far away from known genes often exhibited specific expression presumably by trapping distal enhancers.
source: PB translocation sites were widely distributed over the genome and lines with insertions far away from known genes often exhibited specific expression presumably by trapping distal enhancers.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the insertion site data presented in Tables 3 and 4.

claim: Distal enhancers are known to regulate tissue specific expression of genes, especially in the forebrain.
source: Distal enhancers are known to regulate tissue specific expression of genes, especially in the forebrain (Nord et al., 2013; 2015; Visel et al., 2009; 2013) and to regulate activity-dependent gene expression (Kim et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on enhancer function.

claim: The results suggest that enhancers are involved in the fine-grained specification of cell types, and that trapping them can cause very restricted expression patterns.
source: Our results suggest that enhancers are also involved in the fine-grained specification of cell types, and that trapping them can cause very restricted expression patterns.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the overall findings of the study.

claim: The use of a transactivator system, rather than a recombinase system, may have contributed to generating specific reporter expression.
source: The use of a transactivator system, rather than a recombinase system, may also have contributed to generating specific reporter expression. Cre-dependent reporter expression will be present regardless of whether cre continues to be expressed, or whether it was only expressed in the labeled cells or their progenitors earlier in development (Harris et al., 2014), while tet reporters will be expressed only when tTA protein continues to be expressed.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying the specificity of the enhancer trap lines.

claim: The screen revealed two major subtypes of corticothalamic pyramidal neurons in layer 6: primary CT neurons and non-primary CT neurons.
source: Our screen revealed two major subtypes of corticothalamic pyramidal neurons in layer 6: primary CT neurons and non-primary CT neurons.
evidence: This is a summary of the layer 6 characterization results.

claim: The two cell types differ in distribution within layer 6 and have distinctive axonal projection patterns in the thalamus.
source: The two cell types differ in distribution within layer 6 and have distinctive axonal projection patterns in the thalamus.
evidence: This summarizes the anatomical differences between the two CT neuron types.

claim: The two CT neuron types have distinct RNA expression profiles identifying marker genes that display almost non-overlapping patterns in layer 6.
source: They also have distinct RNA expression profiles identifying marker genes that display almost non-overlapping patterns in layer 6.
evidence: This summarizes the RNAseq and in situ hybridization results.

claim: Genetic labeling of primary CT cells by Ntsr1-Cre has greatly advanced understandings of functions of layer 6 primary CT in cortical and thalamic circuits.
source: Genetic labeling of primary CT cells by Ntsrt1-Cre (Gong et al., 2007) has greatly advanced understandings of functions of layer 6 primary CT in cortical (Bortone et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2014; Olsen et al., 2012) and thalamic (Crandall et al., 2015) circuits.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple functional studies using Ntsr1-Cre.

claim: 56L cells in SSp had projection to multiple nuclei (VPM, Po and ILM) as originally described by Zhang and Deschenes.
source: We found that 56L cells in SSp had projection to multiple nuclei (VPM, Po and ILM) as originally described by Zhang and Deschenes (Zhang and Deschenes, 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by the viral tracing data and citation to Zhang and Deschenes, 1997.

claim: 56L in SSs has strong projections to VPM, which implies there are previously unidentified sources of CT feedback from higher order cortical regions to primary sensory thalamic nuclei.
source: 56L in SSs has strong projections to VPM, which implies there are previously unidentified sources of CT feedback from higher order cortical regions to primary sensory thalamic nuclei (Sherman, 2012; Thomson, 2010).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the projection data with citations to relevant reviews.
